questions.question: A pipeline increases its batch size to process more events per second overall. What is the most likely effect on any single event's end-to-end latency?

choices.text: It decreases, since batching reduces per-event overhead
It increases, since an event may wait for its batch to fill
It stays exactly the same regardless of batch size
It becomes unpredictable and cannot be reasoned about

questions.explanation: Larger batches improve throughput by amortizing fixed overhead across more events, but an individual event now has to wait for the batch to fill (or a timeout) before being processed, raising its own latency. (a) confuses throughput gains with per-item latency. (c) ignores the queuing effect entirely. (d) overstates the uncertainty — the relationship is a well-understood, direct trade-off, not chaos.

questions.question: Per Eric Brewer's own clarification of the CAP theorem, when does a system actually have to choose between consistency and availability?

choices.text: Only for the small subset of read operations, never for writes
Continuously, since all three properties are always in direct tension
Only during an active network partition between nodes
Only once the dataset exceeds a single node's storage capacity

questions.explanation: Brewer clarified that partition tolerance isn't optional in practice, so the real trade-off is consistency vs. availability, and specifically only while a partition is occurring. Outside a partition, there's no forced trade-off. (a) invents a read/write distinction CAP doesn't make. (b) is the popular but incorrect 'always in tension' reading Brewer explicitly rejected. (d) confuses CAP with a scaling/sharding concern.

questions.question: What specific trade-off does the PACELC theorem add on top of CAP?

choices.text: Latency vs. consistency, applying during normal, non-partitioned operation
A fourth property, Performance, that must be balanced against C, A, and P
A requirement that all replicas be geographically co-located
Durability vs. availability, applying only during a partition

questions.explanation: PACELC's 'Else' branch says that even absent a partition, a system must still trade latency against consistency (synchronous replication for consistency costs latency). (b) misreads the 'P' in PACELC as a fourth property rather than 'Partitioned'. (c) is unrelated to what PACELC describes. (d) swaps in the wrong property pair and the wrong condition (PACELC's partition branch reuses CAP's C/A choice, not durability).

questions.question: In a quorum-replicated store with N=5 replicas, which (W, R) pair fails to guarantee that reads see the latest write?
questions.explanation: The overlap guarantee requires W + R > N. With N=5: (a) 3+3=6>5 holds; (b) 4+2=6>5 holds; (d) 5+1=6>5 holds. Only (c) 2+2=4, which is not greater than 5, so a read and write quorum can fail to share a replica and a read can miss the latest write.

questions.question: What specific problem does consistent hashing solve compared to plain `hash(key) % N`?

choices.text: It makes hash computation itself faster on modern CPUs
It bounds how many keys must move when N changes, instead of remapping nearly all of them
It eliminates the need for any replication across nodes
It guarantees keys are always sorted in insertion order across nodes

questions.explanation: With mod-N hashing, changing N changes almost every key's assignment; consistent hashing's ring structure means only the keys near the changed node's ring segment move — roughly a 1/N fraction. (a) is not what the technique addresses (it's about remapping, not raw hash speed). (c) and (d) describe unrelated properties consistent hashing doesn't provide.

questions.question: Using Brendan Gregg's USE method to triage a slow service, what does high 'saturation' on a resource specifically indicate?

choices.text: The resource is returning malformed responses to some requests
The resource has been replaced or restarted recently
Work is queued waiting because the resource can't service it fast enough
The resource's error rate has exceeded a fixed alerting threshold

questions.explanation: Saturation specifically measures queued/waiting demand a resource can't immediately service — separate from utilization (busy time) and errors (which (a) and (d) describe). (b) isn't a USE method concept at all.

questions.question: By Amdahl's Law, if 25% of a workload must run sequentially, what is the maximum possible speedup from adding unlimited parallel processors to the rest?

choices.text: Unlimited — enough processors eventually approach infinite speedup
4x, since maximum speedup is the reciprocal of the sequential fraction
25x, matching the sequential percentage directly
75x, matching the parallelizable percentage directly

questions.explanation: Max speedup = 1 / (sequential fraction) = 1 / 0.25 = 4x. (a) ignores that the sequential portion sets a hard floor on total time no matter how much parallel capacity is added. (c) and (d) misapply the percentages directly rather than taking the reciprocal.

questions.question: A downstream service genuinely cannot handle bursts of traffic even briefly and needs a strictly constant inbound request rate. Which rate-limiting algorithm best fits that requirement?

choices.text: Token bucket, since it allows accumulated bursts up to its capacity
Leaky bucket, since it forwards requests at a fixed, constant output rate
Fixed window counter, since it resets predictably every interval
No rate limiter is needed if the client is trusted

questions.explanation: Leaky bucket forwards requests at a strictly constant rate regardless of how bursty arrivals are, queuing or dropping the excess — exactly what a burst-intolerant downstream needs. (a) is the opposite behavior (bursts are explicitly allowed). (c) still permits a boundary-burst doubling effect across window edges. (d) ignores that the requirement is about downstream capacity, not trust.

questions.question: A team's access patterns are still unknown and they expect to need frequent ad hoc joins across entities. Which database category is the safer default?

choices.text: A relational (SQL) database
A NoSQL database, since it will scale better later regardless
Whichever has lower list-price licensing cost
A NoSQL database, since schemas can't be changed once chosen

questions.explanation: Relational databases defer the 'how will this be queried' decision to query time via joins and ad hoc filtering, which fits unknown/evolving access patterns; most NoSQL stores instead require committing to access patterns via the partition/sort key design up front. (b) and (d) both push NoSQL for the wrong or backwards reasons. (c) ignores the actual technical fit entirely.

questions.question: Two application instances behind a load balancer both run in the same single Availability Zone. What single point of failure remains?

choices.text: None — two instances behind a load balancer is fully redundant
The load balancer's DNS entry, which never changes
The Availability Zone itself, whose failure takes down both instances
The application code, if it was written by a single engineer

questions.explanation: Instance-level redundancy doesn't protect against a failure of the shared fault-isolation zone (the AZ) they both run in — true resilience requires spreading across independent zones. (a) misses this shared-domain risk. (b) and (d) aren't the fault-isolation concern this scenario is testing.

questions.question: What actually distinguishes a microservice from a well-factored module inside a monolith?

choices.text: It has cleaner internal code organization than the rest of the app
It can be deployed, scaled, and can fail independently
The microservice is written in a stricter programming language
The microservice has a smaller total amount of code

questions.explanation: The distinguishing factor is the deployment/failure boundary, not code cleanliness — a module can be just as well-organized but still shares the monolith's process, deploy cycle, and database. (a) describes something either can have; (c) and (d) aren't actual distinguishing properties of microservices at all.

questions.question: In Domain-Driven Design, what is a "bounded context"?

choices.text: A network boundary enforced by a firewall between two services
The maximum number of entities allowed in one database table
The boundary where one domain model has one consistent meaning
A limit on how many services one team is allowed to own

questions.explanation: A bounded context is a modeling boundary, not an infrastructure or organizational limit — inside it, terms like "Product" mean one specific thing. (a), (b), and (d) invent constraints DDD doesn't define.

questions.question: Why can't a business operation spanning multiple microservices typically be wrapped in one ACID transaction?

choices.text: REST APIs don't support returning error codes across services
Each service owns its own database, so there's no shared commit point
Kubernetes disables transactions by default for security reasons
HTTP requests are capped at one write operation per request

questions.explanation: Database-per-service means there's no shared transactional resource to coordinate an atomic commit/rollback across, which is exactly the gap the Saga pattern fills with local transactions plus compensations. The other options aren't real constraints in play here.

questions.question: What's the defining difference between a choreography-based saga and an orchestration-based saga?

choices.text: Choreography can only be used with exactly two services
Orchestration is always faster since it makes fewer network calls
Choreography requires a shared database between all participants
Choreography reacts to events with no coordinator; orchestration uses one

questions.explanation: That's the core mechanical difference — no coordinator vs. a central one tracking and driving the flow. (a) and (c) are fabricated constraints, and (b) isn't a general truth (orchestration adds a coordinator hop, it doesn't inherently reduce calls).

questions.question: In client-side service discovery, who queries the service registry to find a healthy instance to call?

choices.text: The DNS server resolving the service's hostname
The calling service itself, before making the request
The database storing the service's persistent data
A human operator, manually, before each deployment

questions.explanation: That's what makes it "client-side" — the caller looks up the registry itself and picks an instance, as opposed to server-side discovery where an intermediary (load balancer/router) does that lookup instead. The other options don't describe how discovery registries are queried.

questions.question: What problem does an API Gateway primarily solve for clients of a microservices system?

choices.text: It encrypts data at rest inside each service's database
It automatically writes unit tests for every backend service
It replaces the need for services to have their own databases
It gives clients one entry point instead of many direct service calls

questions.explanation: The gateway proxies or composes requests so a client makes one call instead of many round trips to individual services. (a), (b), and (c) describe things an API Gateway doesn't do.

questions.question: In distributed tracing, what is a "span"?

choices.text: The total number of services a request can pass through before timing out
One unit of work within a trace, with its own timing and metadata
A fixed time window used to batch log entries for shipping
The maximum allowed depth of nested service calls

questions.explanation: A span captures one operation's timing and metadata; a trace is the full chain of spans for one logical request across services. The other options aren't real tracing concepts.

questions.question: What is a "distributed monolith"?

choices.text: A monolith that has been deployed to multiple geographic regions
A single service that internally mixes multiple programming languages
Services split across the network but still coupled enough to deploy together
A database replicated across more than one data center

questions.explanation: It's services that are physically separate but functionally still coupled — often via shared internal libraries or technical-layer splits — so you pay the network/operational cost of a distributed system without gaining independent deployability. The other options describe unrelated concepts (multi-region deployment, polyglot code, DB replication).

questions.question: Why does the shared-database anti-pattern undermine microservices' benefits?

choices.text: It forces cross-service reads to run in a different programming language
It doubles the storage cost of every table involved
It lets services bypass each other's rules and couples their schemas
It is disallowed by most cloud providers' terms of service

questions.explanation: Sharing a database means any service can read/write another's data directly, bypassing its owning service's rules, and a schema change now has to consider every consumer — reintroducing exactly the coupling database-per-service is meant to remove. The other options aren't real consequences of this anti-pattern.

questions.question: What does Conway's Law state?

choices.text: System designs tend to mirror their organization's communication structure
Software projects always take longer than initially estimated
Distributed systems eventually converge to a monolithic architecture
A system's bug count is proportional to its number of services

questions.explanation: Conway's original claim is that organizations are constrained to produce designs that copy their own communication structure — which is why service boundaries often end up matching team boundaries by default. (b) describes Hofstadter's Law, and (c)/(d) aren't established principles.

questions.question: In Clean Architecture's Dependency Rule, which direction must source-code dependencies point?

choices.text: Bidirectionally, as long as no cycles exist between layers
Inward, toward entities and use cases only
It depends on which layer initiates the request at runtime
Outward, from entities toward frameworks and drivers

questions.explanation: The Dependency Rule requires source-code dependencies to point inward only, toward higher-level policy (entities, use cases) — outer layers may reference inner ones, never the reverse, even though runtime control flow can go outward via interfaces defined by the inner layer. Allowing dependencies in either direction defeats the rule's purpose; claiming direction depends on which layer initiates the request confuses runtime call direction with compile-time dependency direction; and requiring dependencies to point outward reverses the rule entirely.

questions.question: In Hexagonal Architecture, what is a "port"?

choices.text: A background job that synchronizes two adapters with each other
The concrete database driver used by a persistence adapter
A network endpoint the application listens on for incoming requests
A tech-agnostic interface for talking to the outside world

questions.explanation: A port is a technology-agnostic interface (like OrderRepository or NotificationSender) representing a purposeful conversation between the application core and something external; adapters are the technology-specific implementations that plug into a port. A concrete database driver is an adapter's implementation detail, not the port itself; a literal network endpoint confuses the term with networking; and a background job synchronizing adapters isn't part of the pattern's vocabulary at all.

questions.question: According to Martin Fowler, CQRS is worth adopting mainly in which situation?

choices.text: Every system, applied uniformly across the whole codebase for consistency
Only systems already using event sourcing for their write model
A complex domain or a big read/write load gap, in one bounded context
Any system where reads and writes touch the same database tables

questions.explanation: Fowler recommends CQRS narrowly: for a specific bounded context with real domain complexity or a significant read/write load imbalance — never applied uniformly system-wide, which he calls risky complexity. Applying it to every system for consistency is the opposite of his "never a whole system" guidance; requiring event sourcing first is false, since CQRS and event sourcing are separable choices; and "reads/writes touch the same tables" isn't the criterion he uses at all.

questions.question: What does an event-sourcing "snapshot" primarily optimize for?

choices.text: Avoiding the need to version event schemas over time
Cuts replay cost by resuming from a saved computed state
Reducing the storage size of the full event log
Guaranteeing strong consistency between the read and write models

questions.explanation: A snapshot periodically persists fully-computed state so a later load only replays events since that snapshot instead of the entire history, cutting replay cost. It doesn't shrink the underlying event log's total storage, doesn't remove the need to version event schemas for events predating the snapshot, and has nothing to do with guaranteeing consistency between CQRS read and write models.

questions.question: What is the defining symptom of an anemic domain model?

choices.text: The domain model has too many small classes instead of a few larger ones
The domain layer imports too many third-party libraries
Business rules are duplicated across multiple microservices
Domain classes are just getters/setters; logic lives in services

questions.explanation: An anemic model has the shape of OO objects but no real behavior — logic lives in separate services that manipulate the data holders from outside, which Fowler says pays a domain model's persistence cost without its behavioral benefit. Having many small classes is a granularity concern, not this pattern; importing too many libraries is a coupling concern; and duplicated rules across microservices is a cross-service consistency problem — neither is specific to anemia.

questions.question: The classic mutable Rectangle/Square example is used to illustrate a violation of which SOLID principle?

choices.text: Liskov Substitution Principle
Open-Closed Principle
Interface Segregation Principle
Single Responsibility Principle

questions.explanation: Square extending a mutable Rectangle (with independent setWidth/setHeight) breaks code written against Rectangle's contract, because setting one dimension on a Square silently changes the other — a behavioral-contract violation, which is exactly what the Liskov Substitution Principle is about. It isn't about extension-without-modification (Open-Closed), interface bloat (Interface Segregation), or a class having multiple reasons to change (Single Responsibility).

questions.question: What problem does the Interface Segregation Principle target that Single Responsibility does not directly address?

choices.text: Whether a subclass can be substituted for its superclass safely
Whether a client depends on interface methods it never uses
Whether a class has more than one reason to change
Whether high-level code depends directly on low-level implementation details

questions.explanation: The Interface Segregation Principle is specifically about not forcing a client to depend on methods it doesn't use, favoring small role-specific interfaces over one fat interface — a concern about interface shape, distinct from Single Responsibility's concern about why a class changes. Safe subclass substitution is Liskov Substitution, and high-level code depending on low-level details is what Dependency Inversion addresses instead.

questions.question: What does Conway's Law claim about the relationship between an organization and the systems it builds?

choices.text: Designs tend to mirror the org's communication structure
Communication overhead decreases as an organization scales its engineering headcount
Larger organizations always ship higher-quality software than smaller ones
Software architecture should be decided independently of team structure for best results

questions.explanation: Conway's Law states that organizations are constrained to produce designs that copy their own communication structure — subsystem boundaries tend to mirror the teams and communication paths that created them. Claiming communication overhead decreases with scale, that larger orgs always ship higher quality, or that architecture should be decided independently of team structure are not claims Conway makes — the last is actually the opposite of the law's implication, since team structure and architecture are entangled whether you plan for it or not.

questions.question: Which of these is the most accurate distinction between a design pattern and an architectural pattern?

choices.text: Design patterns only apply to Java; architectural patterns are language-agnostic
Architectural patterns are always faster to implement than design patterns
Design patterns are class-level, architectural patterns are system-wide
Design patterns require a framework, architectural patterns don't

questions.explanation: Design patterns (Strategy, Observer, Adapter, etc.) address recurring problems at the scale of a few collaborating classes; architectural patterns (layered, hexagonal, microservices, CQRS) govern how components or services across the whole system communicate, and are far more expensive to reverse. Claiming one category is always faster, that design patterns are Java-specific, or that one requires a framework and the other doesn't are not real distinguishing properties between the two.

questions.question: Which of the following are legitimate reasons Clean/Hexagonal Architecture's full layering can be over-engineering for a given application? (select all that apply)

choices.text: The team currently has fewer than five engineers assigned to the codebase
The application never needs to be deployed to more than one server
The application is thin CRUD with no real business logic to isolate from infrastructure
There is no realistic scenario where the database or framework will be swapped

questions.explanation: The real justification for the extra layering is proportional to how much genuine business logic needs isolating and how likely infrastructure is to change — neither of which holds for thin CRUD apps with a fixed tech stack, making those two legitimate reasons to skip the ceremony. Team size and single-server deployment aren't the relevant factors — a small team with genuinely complex business rules can still benefit, and deployment topology is unrelated to this architectural choice.
